title: The history of the termite mound
tagline: From a naturalist's 1781 letter to robots and solar-powered breathing: how people worked out what a termite mound does.
intro: For two centuries people admired termite mounds without knowing how they work. In 1961 the mound became the textbook "air-conditioned nest", and an architect in Zimbabwe built a city block on that idea. Field measurements since then have shown the mound is more like a lung that breathes with the sun and the wind, and some questions are still open.

eras.name: Wonder and use
eras.summary: Naturalists describe the giant mounds, and people across Africa use mound clay to build and to smelt iron.

eras.name: The air-conditioned nest
eras.summary: Scientists picture the mound as a chimney that sheds colony heat, and an architect builds on the idea.

eras.name: A lung, not an air conditioner
eras.summary: Field measurements show mounds mainly swap gases with the air, and that the colony is an ancient fungus farm.

eras.name: Breathing with the sun
eras.summary: New sensors, X-rays and robots show mounds are ventilated by daily heating and gusts, and inspire new ways to build.

eras.name: Mounds in deep time
eras.summary: Dating shows some mounds have been lived in for thousands, even tens of thousands, of years.

events.title: A naturalist describes Africa's giant termite mounds
events.text: Smeathman spent four years studying insects around Sierra Leone from 1771. In 1781 his letter on termites was read to the Royal Society and printed with engravings of his paintings. He described West African mounds over 12 feet tall.
events.why: It was the first detailed European account of the huge mounds and the insects that build them.

events.title: Iron smelters build furnaces on termite mounds
events.who: Iron workers of Chongwe, studied by Edwinus Lyaya and colleagues
events.text: At Chongwe, every iron smelting site found sat on a termite mound, with three or four furnaces on the west side of each one. The furnace chimneys stood up to about three metres tall, and their walls were probably made from mound clay.
events.why: It shows people using termite-built clay as a tough, heat-resistant building material.

events.title: Lüscher works out how much air a colony needs
events.text: Lüscher calculated that a large colony needs at least about 240 litres of oxygen a day. That means about 1,200 litres of air must reach the nest every day.
events.why: It showed that a buried nest has a real breathing problem to solve.

events.title: Grassé names "stigmergy"
events.text: Grassé watched termites rebuild their nest. Each worker reacted to what the others had already built, not to orders. He called this work-triggers-work idea stigmergy.
events.why: It explained how millions of insects with no plan can still build one mound.

events.title: The "air-conditioned termite nest"
events.text: Lüscher argued that heat from the colony makes warm air rise up a central shaft. Cooler air then returns through channels near the surface. The article reached a wide audience.
events.why: This thermosiphon picture became the textbook story, and later work challenged it.

events.title: Cathedral mounds and dome mounds
events.text: The same species, Macrotermes bellicosus, builds tall ridged "cathedral" mounds in open savanna. In shaded forest it builds thick-walled "dome" mounds.
events.why: It hinted that mound shape changes with the local climate.

events.title: An 8.7 metre mound is photographed in Somalia
events.text: A mound about 8.7 metres tall was photographed in Somalia. Guinness World Records notes it as a one-off case in its archive.
events.why: It gives a sense of how tall the biggest mounds can get.

events.title: Turning a "magnetic" mound makes it overheat
events.text: Some Australian termites build flat mounds that face north and south. Grigg found the nest stayed at about 33 to 35 °C through the day. When he cut a mound free and turned it east-west, it reached 40 to 42 °C.
events.why: It showed that mound shape and direction can control nest temperature.

events.title: Turner starts probing mounds in Namibia
events.text: Turner began decades of fieldwork on Macrotermes mounds. He filled mounds with propane to trace air, scanned them with lasers and filled them with plaster to cast the tunnels.
events.why: His casts and tracer tests gave the first clear pictures of air paths inside mounds.

events.title: Magnetic mounds point slightly different ways
events.text: Jacklyn measured many magnetic mounds. Their average direction changed from place to place, from true north near the coast to 10° east further south. He linked this to keeping the east face at a steady temperature.
events.why: It showed termites tune mound direction to local sun, wind and shade.

events.title: The Eastgate Centre opens in Harare
events.who: Mick Pearce, Arup and Old Mutual Properties
events.text: Architect Mick Pearce designed a large office and shopping block that cools itself without conventional air conditioning. It stores heat in its heavy structure by day and flushes it out with night air through 48 brick chimneys. Pearce named the termite mound as his model.
events.why: Arup calls it the first large modern building in Southern Africa cooled this way.

events.title: Measuring a mound's breath in Kenya
events.who: J. P. E. C. Darlington and colleagues
events.text: The team measured gases leaving whole nests of Macrotermes jeanneli. A large nest gave off about 100,000 to 400,000 litres of gas a day, including 800 to 1,500 litres of carbon dioxide. Most of the water it lost came from the soil.
events.why: It put real numbers on how much a colony breathes.

events.title: Savanna mounds versus forest mounds
events.who: Judith Korb and K. Eduard Linsenmair
events.text: In open savanna, big Macrotermes bellicosus nests stayed near 30 °C, changing by less than 2 °C while the air outside swung by about 35 °C. In cooler forest, nests averaged about 28 °C. When trees were cut and the site got warmer, the termites built more ridged mounds.
events.why: It showed the mound trades off keeping heat in against letting stale air out.

events.title: Day and night airflow in cathedral mounds
events.who: Judith Korb and K. Eduard Linsenmair
events.text: By day, air rose in channels inside the sunny ridges and pulled stale air out of the nest. At night the pattern flipped and warm air rose up the central shaft. Carbon dioxide was low by day and higher at night.
events.why: It showed outside temperature, not just colony heat, drives the airflow.

events.title: "The Extended Organism" is published
events.text: Turner's book treats structures that animals build, such as termite mounds, as organs outside the body. It is about the physiology of animal-built structures.
events.why: It framed the mound as part of the colony's body, not just a house.

events.title: The mound as a lung
events.text: Turner found that Macrotermes michaelseni mounds do not control nest temperature in the way people had assumed. He argued the mound mainly helps the colony swap oxygen and carbon dioxide, driven by gusty wind. He called mounds "accessory organs of gas exchange".
events.why: It shifted the question from cooling to breathing.

events.title: Fungus farming began once, in Africa
events.who: Duur Aanen, Corinne Rouland-Lefèvre and colleagues
events.text: DNA from termites and their Termitomyces fungi showed the partnership started once, in Africa. The fungi have never gone back to living on their own. About 330 fungus-growing termite species are known.
events.why: It showed the mound exists to serve an ancient farm.

events.title: Termite mushrooms on the menu
events.text: An FAO review lists about 20 edible Termitomyces species from Africa and Asia. They are collected, sold in markets and along roadsides, and are a good source of income. Termitomyces titanicus is described as the world's largest edible fungus.
events.why: The fungus the mound protects is also food for people.

events.title: "Beyond biomimicry"
events.who: J. Scott Turner and Rupert Soar
events.text: A biologist and an engineer argued that buildings should do more than copy termite shapes. They wanted buildings that are, in a sense, as alive as the people in them. Their research suggested mounds do not mainly regulate temperature.
events.why: It questioned the popular story behind termite-inspired buildings.

events.title: Termite farming is dated to about 31 million years ago
events.who: T. Nobre, N. A. Koné, S. Konaté, K. E. Linsenmair and Duur Aanen
events.text: Using DNA, the team estimated that fungus-growing termites arose in African rainforest about 31 million years ago, with a range of 19 to 49 million. This was shortly before savannas spread.
events.why: Termites were farming fungus long before people farmed anything.

events.title: Robots build like termites
events.who: Justin Werfel, Kirstin Petersen and Radhika Nagpal
events.text: The TERMES robots build towers and pyramids from foam bricks with no leader and no messages. Each robot follows simple rules and reacts to the structure as it grows. The idea came from termites in Namibia.
events.why: It showed that stigmergy can be used to build things on purpose.

events.title: Eating termite mound soil in pregnancy
events.text: In a survey of 340 pregnant women, 45.6% said they ate soil. Most of the soil samples they ate came from termite mounds. The study warned some samples held high levels of chemical elements.
events.why: Mound clay is part of daily life, and of health questions, in parts of Africa.

events.title: Mounds breathe with the daily heat cycle
events.who: Hunter King, Samuel Ocko and L. Mahadevan
events.text: The team measured air inside about 25 mounds of Odontotermes obesus. By day the thin outer flutes warm faster than the core, so air rises in them and sinks in the chimney. At night it reverses. Carbon dioxide built up to nearly 6% in the nest by day and was flushed out at night.
events.why: It showed the daily swing in outside temperature, not wind or colony heat, drives the flow.

events.title: African mounds are solar powered too
events.who: Samuel Ocko, J. Scott Turner, Rupert Soar, L. Mahadevan and colleagues
events.text: The team measured air speed and temperature inside Macrotermes michaelseni mounds in sunny Namibia. Sun heating again drove air flows that reversed between day and night. Carbon dioxide stayed close to 5% in the mound.
events.why: It showed solar ventilation works in very different termites and climates.

events.title: Two hundred million mounds seen from space
events.who: Stephen Martin, Roy Funch, Paul Hanson and Eun-Hye Yoo
events.text: About 200 million evenly spaced mounds, each about 2.5 m tall, cover some 230,000 km². They are spoil heaps from tunnels dug by Syntermes dirus. Soil from 11 mounds dated from 690 to 3,820 years old.
events.why: Termite building can last for thousands of years and reshape a whole landscape.

events.title: X-rays reveal pores in mound walls
events.where: Imperial College London, UK (nests from Senegal and Guinea)
events.text: 3D X-ray images showed linked networks of larger and smaller pores in termite nest walls. The pores let carbon dioxide out, insulate like double glazing, and drain rain by capillary action.
events.why: It showed the wall itself is a breathing skin.

events.title: Open and closed mounds run at different temperatures
events.text: Closed mounds of Macrotermes michaelseni were mostly warmer than open mounds of M. subhyalinus. Termitomyces fungus grows best at about 29 to 30 °C, and one fungus type was found mainly in warmer mounds.
events.why: Mound design and the fungus it grows are matched.

events.title: Humidity guides where termites build
events.who: Paul Bardunias, Rupert Soar, J. Scott Turner, Radhika Nagpal, Justin Werfel and colleagues
events.text: Air in the mound's tunnels was about 93% humid. Termites built outward where the moist air reached past the soil surface. The fungus needs a narrow range of humidity.
events.why: It linked mound growth to keeping the nest moist.

events.title: A tunnel maze that breathes with the wind
events.where: Lund, Sweden and Nottingham, UK (mounds in Namibia)
events.text: Macrotermes michaelseni mounds have an "egress complex", a lattice of tunnels 3 to 5 mm wide near the surface. Tests on a 3D-printed copy showed that small back-and-forth air movements, like gusty wind, can carry gas and moisture through it.
events.why: Wind may still help mounds breathe, and the idea could shape building walls.

events.title: Mounds tens of thousands of years old
events.text: Radiocarbon dating of mounds built by the southern harvester termite gave ages of about 13,000 to 19,000 years for organic carbon. Carbonate in them dated back up to about 34,000 years.
events.why: They are the oldest inhabited termite mounds known.

people.name: Henry Smeathman
people.note: Wrote the 1781 Royal Society account of African termites after four years in Sierra Leone.

people.name: Edwinus Lyaya
people.role: Archaeologist, University of Dar es Salaam
people.note: Studied iron-smelting furnaces built on termite mounds in Zambia and Tanzania.

people.name: Martin Lüscher
people.note: Proposed the "air-conditioned" thermosiphon model of the termite nest.

people.name: Pierre-Paul Grassé
people.note: Coined the word stigmergy for building guided by the work already done.

people.name: Mick Pearce
people.note: Designed the termite-inspired, passively cooled Eastgate Centre in Harare.

people.name: Judith Korb
people.note: Showed how Macrotermes bellicosus mounds differ between savanna and forest in Côte d'Ivoire.

people.name: J. Scott Turner
people.role: Physiologist, SUNY College of Environmental Science and Forestry
people.note: Recast the mound as a lung for gas exchange, using tracer gas and plaster casts in Namibia.

people.name: Radhika Nagpal
people.note: Led the TERMES project on termite-inspired robot builders.

people.name: Kirstin Petersen
people.role: Roboticist, then a Harvard graduate student
people.note: Designed and built the TERMES robots and their bricks.

people.name: L. Mahadevan
people.note: Led the studies showing mounds breathe with the daily temperature cycle in India and Namibia.

people.name: Michele Francis
people.note: Led the dating of Namaqualand mounds up to about 34,000 years old.

series.title: How tall the mounds in these studies were
series.caption: Heights reported in studies over time; they vary with species and place, not with the year.

points.label: Sierra Leone: over 12 feet, about 3.7 m (Smeathman)
Namibia: about 5 m or higher (National Geographic)
India, Odontotermes obesus: about 2 m (King et al.)
Namibia, Macrotermes michaelseni: up to 3 m (Ocko et al.)
Brazil, Syntermes dirus: about 2.5 m (Martin et al.)
Kenya: tallest studied mound 1.75 m (Vesala et al.)

facts: A big Macrotermes nest in Kenya breathed out about 800 to 1,500 litres of carbon dioxide a day.
In savanna mounds in Côte d'Ivoire, the nest stayed near 30 °C, changing by less than 2 °C while outside air swung by about 35 °C.
Inside the mound, the fungus takes up about eight times more space than the termites and does about 85% of the breathing.
Brazil's 200 million Syntermes mounds hold about 10 cubic kilometres of soil, roughly 4,000 Great Pyramids of Giza.
By day, carbon dioxide in an Indian termite nest can build up to nearly 6%.
